rv.q: John J. Caswell Jr.'s 'Wet Brain,' at Playwrights Horizons, is also a very funny, pitch-black comedy about addiction and obligation, love and abandonment, and patterns of poisonous behavior lodged so deep they seem encoded.
The story is harrowing, heartening, and, eventually, surrealistic in a manner that I've never seen achieved onstage.
Dustin Wills' subtle direction perfectly balances kitchen-sink realism with the bizarre elements creating an endearingly off-kilter, but ultimately healing family drama, unlike any other.

His inspired direction of Caswell’s play is a wild ride, and the play itself, “Wet Brain,” which had its world premiere Thursday at Playwrights Horizons Tuesday, gives this gifted director plenty of opportunities to go completely off the rails in a very good way.
Wet Brain , co-produced by Playwrights Horizons and MCC Theater, offers a gripping, grating look at alcoholism and its effects on loved ones.
It is easier to appreciate “Wet Brain” by treating the sci fi aspects as a metaphor, one that the playwright might have imagined to help him deal with his own trauma.
It is moments like this that prove that while Wet Brain might be an imperfect play, it has vital lessons to offer us and is a compelling portrait of dysfunction.
But as satisfying as it is to see these characters confront their past and resolve what needs to be resolved, the hour preceding that revelatory scene drags at times...
For him to tackle such personal material so early in his career is almost recklessly courageous, but he may have taken on a challenge for which he is not yet ready.

Wet Brain, a deceptively engaging play by John J. Caswell, Jr., is certainly a catchier title than what it refers to, Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (WKS), which is a brain disorder related to the acute and chronic phases of a vitamin B1 (Thiamine) deficiency.
Near the end of the play, we enter one of Joe’s hallucinations in a stunning coup de theatre moment that is visually captivating but dramatically rather hollow.
The scenarios are far out, but lack a compelling emotional center.
Wet Brain falls short of both logic and illogic.

But its often overwrought acting and uncomfortable mingling of gritty naturalism and fantastical confession throw a wet blanket on a work that should make one feel more deeply than this one does for its largely unsympathetic characters’ dilemmas.

cn.t: Critics find this dysfunctional family drama ambitious and genre-bending, with standout scenic design and strong performances elevating its exploration of addiction and trauma, though some wish the one-act had more room to fully develop its surreal storytelling.
